Quantitative Assessment of Failure and Fault Modes The fault reconnaissance study systematically evaluated failure mechanisms across six major WEC subsystems: generator, power electronic switches, WEC body, mooring lines, O-rings/seals, and PTO. Each failure mode was ranked on a 1-5 scale for both probability and severity, with severity quantified in dollars per year based on work time, crew requirements, vessel costs, and lost revenue for a 100 kW reference WEC. Biofouling on the WEC body emerged as a high-risk item at approximately $204,000/year, driven by inevitable marine growth reaching 100% coverage within 500 days and causing up to 45% power reduction. PTO failures are a roughly $254,000/year risk due to system complexity requiring extensive repair time and potential drydocking. The analysis also identified corrosion as a prevalent failure mechanism across multiple components, with O-ring and seal corrosion presenting approximately $96,000/year in risk due to accelerated degradation in saltwater environments. Extreme sea states posed $169,000/year risk to mooring systems. Fault Mitigation and Control Strategies Both studies explored adaptive control to compensate for biofouling-induced model mismatch. For point absorbers, re-optimizing PTO damping for biofouled conditions recovered 2 kW of a 32 kW loss (approximately 6% of the degradation), demonstrating that biofouling effects are largely irreducible through damping control alone. For hydrokinetic turbines, a SARSA reinforcement learning controller using Gaussian radial basis function approximation was developed that continuously learns optimal damping coefficients as plant dynamics change. Tested against Mississippi River flow data over one year with progressive biofouling, the RL controller generated 0.92% more energy than a fixed optimal-TSR baseline by adapting to the shifting Cp curve without requiring explicit biofouling measurement. This demonstrates that adaptive control strategies can partially mitigate performance degradation from marine growth. 8 Recommendations Future work should explore more detailed biofouling models that account for species-specific growth patterns and spatial distribution. Additionally, the RM3 model could consider ballasting, to change the hydrodynamic behavior of the system in response to the impacts of biofouling. This is a good topic for future research. Experimental validation of simulation results would strengthen confidence in the models. Adaptive control strategies, such as reinforcement learning, should be further developed and tested in hardware-in-the-loop or field environments. These methods show promise for improving performance under fault conditions. Design guidelines should incorporate fault reconnaissance findings to improve system resilience. Maintenance strategies should consider the trade-offs between physical cleaning and control adaptation. Dissemination of these findings through technical publications and collaboration with industry partners will help accelerate the adoption of robust control methods in marine renewable energy systems. The two main published products from the work are the American Controls Conference papers by Skrovanek and Barton. Both were presented at a special session of the 2024 ACC meeting. 9 Award Outputs Technologies or Techniques – Biofouling modeling techniques for both WECs and MCTs, along with preliminary implemention of reinforcement learning based control.
